name: Learn: Cluster Hardening
description: Learn node-level CKS cluster hardening step by step on a real multi-node cluster: control-plane manifest file permissions, disabling the kubelet read-only port, the apiserver NodeRestriction admission plugin, least-privilege RBAC, and ServiceAccount token hardening.
objective: CKS › Cluster + System Hardening (15% + 15%). Goal: harden the cluster — manifest file perms, kubelet flags, apiserver admission plugins, and least-privilege RBAC.

questions.title: Harden control-plane file permissions
questions.teach:
Static pod manifests under `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` hold sensitive flags, so CIS wants them mode `0600` (`rw-------`), readable only by root. Use `chmod 600 <file>` and verify with `stat -c '%a' <file>`. On a kind cluster each node is a container, so run it via `docker exec <node> ...`.

**Gotcha:** Changing a manifest's mode/owner does NOT restart its pod (safe live); only editing its *contents* does.
questions.prompt:
The kube-scheduler static pod manifest on control-plane node `$CP` was left world/group readable at mode `644`. Set `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` on `$CP` to exactly mode `600`.

Target: `docker exec $CP stat -c '%a' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` prints `600`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml   # 600 root:root

questions.title: Disable the kubelet read-only port
questions.teach:
The kubelet's **read-only port** (`10255`) serves pod/node metadata with no auth and no TLS. CIS requires it off: set `readOnlyPort: 0` in the kubelet config (`/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`), then `systemctl restart kubelet`. Any non-zero value leaves it enabled.

**Gotcha:** The config edit does nothing until you restart the kubelet, and the node goes `NotReady` briefly — wait ~20s and confirm it's `Ready` again.
questions.prompt:
On worker `$W1` the kubelet is serving its read-only port (seeded as `readOnlyPort: 10255`). Edit `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` on `$W1` so that `readOnlyPort: 0`, then restart the kubelet. Give the node ~20s to report `Ready` again.

Target: the config on `$W1` has `readOnlyPort: 0` AND node `$W1` is `Ready`.
questions.hint: `docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`, then `docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
docker exec $W1 grep readOnlyPort /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   # readOnlyPort: 0
docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get node $W1   # wait ~20s for Ready

verification.description: node $W1 is still Ready after the kubelet restart

questions.title: Re-enable the NodeRestriction admission plugin
questions.teach:
`NodeRestriction` is an apiserver **admission controller** limiting each kubelet to modifying only its own Node and the Pods bound to it. Enable it in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` via `--enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,...`, appending to any existing comma-separated value as one flag.

**Gotcha:** Saving the manifest auto-restarts the apiserver; a typo takes it DOWN. Wait ~20–60s for it to come back.
questions.prompt:
Setup removed `NodeRestriction` from the apiserver's `--enable-admission-plugins`. Edit `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` on `$CP` so the flag includes `NodeRestriction` again (keep any other plugins), then wait for the apiserver to come back.

Target: the running kube-apiserver has `NodeRestriction` in `--enable-admission-plugins`.
questions.hint: `docker exec -it $CP bash`, then add the line `- --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction` under the kube-apiserver command args (or append `,NodeRestriction` to an existing value). Save and wait ~20s for the apiserver to restart.
questions.solution:
# Setup removed the flag line, so add it back under the kube-apiserver args:
docker exec $CP sed -i '/^    - kube-apiserver$/a\    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# (If the flag already exists with other plugins, instead append ,NodeRestriction to its value.)
# Wait ~20s for the apiserver to restart, then verify:
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins

questions.title: Least-privilege RBAC for a workload
questions.teach:
Give a workload the minimum API access: a narrow namespaced **Role** (only the verbs/resources needed) bound to its ServiceAccount via a **RoleBinding** — never `cluster-admin`. Imperatively: `kubectl create role <r> --verb=get,list --resource=pods` then `kubectl create rolebinding <rb> --role=<r> --serviceaccount=<ns>:<name>`.

**Gotcha:** `--serviceaccount` takes `ns:name`, not just the name.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-learn` a ServiceAccount `reader` already exists. Create a Role granting only `get,list` on `pods` and a RoleBinding binding it to that SA.

Target: SA `reader` can `list pods` (`yes`) but cannot `delete pods` (`no`) in `cks-learn`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n cks-learn create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods`, then `kubectl -n cks-learn create rolebinding reader-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=cks-learn:reader`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n cks-learn create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods
kubectl -n cks-learn create rolebinding reader-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=cks-learn:reader
kubectl auth can-i list pods   --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:reader -n cks-learn   # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:reader -n cks-learn   # no

verification.description: SA reader can list pods but cannot delete pods in cks-learn

questions.title: ServiceAccount token hardening
questions.teach:
By default every pod auto-mounts a ServiceAccount token the attacker could steal. For pods that never call the API, set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the **ServiceAccount** so pods using it get no token volume, and point the pod at it with `serviceAccountName`.

**Gotcha:** `automountServiceAccountToken` sits at the **top level** of the SA object, not inside a `spec:` block — a common YAML mistake.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-learn`, create a ServiceAccount `no-token` with `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, then run a pod `hardened` using that ServiceAccount (image `busybox:1.36`, e.g. `sleep 3600`).

Target: SA `no-token` has `automountServiceAccountToken: false` AND pod `hardened` runs as SA `no-token` with no SA token volume mounted.
questions.hint: Create the SA, patch/set `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, then create the pod with `serviceAccountName: no-token`. Apply a manifest with `kubectl apply -f -`.
questions.solution:
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: no-token
  namespace: cks-learn
automountServiceAccountToken: false
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hardened
  namespace: cks-learn
spec:
  serviceAccountName: no-token
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
YAML

verification.description: SA no-token has automount disabled and pod hardened uses it with no token mounted
